Actual Article Body:
What changes when you swap the daily doomscroll for journalism that asks not just what’s wrong, but what’s working? Oliver Balch finds out

What changes when you swap the daily doomscroll for journalism that asks not just what’s wrong, but what’s working? Oliver Balch finds out

I thought two days without bad news would be easy.

“48 hours,” my editor said. “No problem- or crisis-focused news. Only solutions-focused or constructive journalism.”

“Sure,” I said. Sign me up.

After all, as assignments go, this didn’t sound too taxing. I don’t have a TV, I’m not on TikTok, I rarely go on YouTube and I ditched X long ago. At least the avoiding-the-bad-news-bit should be straightforward.

Wrong.

It turns out I consume far more negativity than I realised.

I choose a weekend for my detox. My logic is simple: less breaking news, less time on my various devices, more time with my head in other, more diverting, pursuits.

It starts well. I feel surprisingly relieved not to be listening to the radio as soon as I wake up. It’s even a bit exhilarating, like I’m breaking some kind of rule. Not waiting for the headline pips, not listening to the professional bickering: it’s also freeing in a way. The silence allows me to take a breath, think about the day ahead, figure out my own mood before the news decides it for me.

Then, after an hour or two, I find myself growing anxious.

The world is unfolding without me.

An itch to reach for the news apps on my phone grows. I resist. (Honestly.) This is ridiculous, I tell myself. Donald Trump doesn’t care whether I’m abreast of his latest Truth Social aberration. I’m not going to make any difference to the Middle East situation by knowing every sub-point of the latest peace plan.

Still, I want to know.

On Monday, after the experiment, I put this to An Nguyen, a visiting professor at Bournemouth University’s Media School and a specialist in digital journalism. He explains that humans have what he describes as an evolutionary “awareness instinct”: a drive to know about potential threats around us. Once, that might have meant spotting a sabre-toothed tiger approaching our cave. Today, it might mean worrying about rogue AI wiping out humanity.

Perhaps, as a news junkie, that explains my anxiety at being shut off from the world around me. But I’m not entirely convinced. AI is scary, but it’s no tiger at the door – at least, not yet. For me, constant news checking is partly distraction, a way of escaping the everyday, and partly titillation: the irresistible pleasure of eavesdropping on the world’s latest drama.

'I started with a healthy dose of What Went Right, straight from Positive News'

Nguyen has another point, though, which I find more convincing – and more reassuring. To be active citizens, he argues, we need to know about the problems around us.

But that leaves me with a question. I follow the news. I know about record temperatures, inequality spikes and social care crises. But then what?

His answer is to get some constructive news into my life.

Fortunately, this tallies with my editor’s instructions.

My first port of call is, naturally, Positive News. I load up the website and click on this week’s edition of the What Went Right roundup. Half an hour later, I’m feeling perky.

This isn’t simply a diet of cheery stories. The section’s bite-sized articles lead me to reports about an EU proposal to ban social media for under-13s, the elimination of dog-transmitted rabies in Chile, a life-extending drug for people with breast cancer in the UK and a fun reward scheme encouraging people in Singapore to read books.

Then my eye is caught by a longer article about the so-called NEETs problem: young people not in education, employment or training. This is where I start to understand the difference between ‘good news’ and constructive journalism.
